case_info.scenario: A 33-year-old woman with a history of hereditary bilateral retinoblastoma as an infant presented to a primary care clinic with 1 week of right lower extremity swelling. At age 8 months, she was treated with right enucleation and left eye radiotherapy (50.4 Gy). At age 4 years, she developed a recurrence of the retinoblastoma in the nasal cavity and was treated with 4 cycles of vincristine, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide followed by 1 cycle of cisplatin, etoposide, and intrathecal cytarabine. Primary care evaluation was prompted by her mother, as the patient had not noticed her lower extremity edema. She had no fevers, weight loss, shortness of breath, chest pain, abdominal pain, or history of deep vein thrombosis. Her physical examination was notable for firm, nonpitting edema to the hip. She did not have any associated tenderness, inguinal lymphadenopathy, or palpable abdominal masses. Her vital signs were within normal limits and she ambulated comfortably. Laboratory work results, including a complete blood cell count with a differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, and D-dimer levels, were within normal limits. Doppler ultrasonography of her right lower extremity showed no deep vein thrombosis. A computed tomography venogram demonstrated a 4.0 × 3.5 cm mass of likely vascular origin that was extending into the right common iliac vein (Figure).
case_info.caption: Computed tomography venogram demonstrating a 4.0 × 3.5 cm heterogeneously enhancing lobulated mass (arrowhead) extending into the right common iliac vein.
case_info.explanation: The patient underwent a transvenous biopsy with an inferior vena cava filter, and pathology results were consistent with a leiomyosarcoma (LMS), grade 3. Computed tomography results of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were negative for metastatic disease. She subsequently underwent a radical resection of the pelvic mass, which revealed a 4-cm mass deriving from and encapsulating the right external iliac vein with R1 margins, which was replaced with an interposition graft. Retinoblastoma is the most common pediatric ocular tumor. The hereditary variant, which is caused by germline variations to the tumor suppressor geneRB1,comprises 40% of all retinoblastoma and is generally associated with bilateral disease.1Long-term survival of these patients is typically excellent; however, there remains a 33.1% risk of developing a secondary cancer.2,3This has important implications for monitoring survivors of hereditary retinoblastoma. The median time to development of a subsequent cancer is 18.9 years, and bone and soft-tissue sarcomas comprise most (40%-60%) subsequent cancers, followed by melanoma, accounting for approximately 10%.3Among soft-tissue sarcomas (STS), LMS is most common, comprising at least 40% of all STS diagnosed in patients with retinoblastoma with a median age at presentation of approximately 32 years.3Other commonly diagnosed subsequent STS include fibrosarcoma, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.3Prior treatment with radiation or chemotherapy may increase the risk of a subsequent cancer.4Radiotherapy is a risk factor for developing a subsequent cancer within the treatment field, and alkylating agents, in particular, seem to increase systemic risk of subsequent cancer. Patients who were treated with radiotherapy and an alkylating agent before age 1 year, as with this patient, may have up to 3.8 times greater risk of developing LMS.4 Leiomyosarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumor that is typically found in the head, neck, thorax, abdomen, retroperitoneum, limbs, uterus, and pelvis of patients with retinoblastoma.3Leiomyosarcoma of large blood vessels comprises approximately 2% of LMS and is often found in the inferior vena cava, femoral, saphenous, jugular, or iliac veins.5 Prognosis is based on histologic grade, tumor size, and tumor depth.6Extrauterine LMS has a 40% 5-year risk of recurrence following resection, and for uterine LMS, the recurrence rates are as high as 70%.6To our knowledge, there are few studies to guide optimal treatment of early-stage disease. Surgical resection is the standard for local disease, and offers a chance at a cure with R0 resection.6Adjuvant radiotherapy in early-stage disease has been shown to decrease the risk of local recurrence; however, a recent large, randomized clinical trial of patients with retroperitoneal LMS demonstrated a limited utility of adjuvant radiotherapy.6,7Adjuvant chemotherapy has not been shown to improve outcomes for patients with uterine LMS.8There have been studies that attempt to risk stratify and identify patients with nonuterine LMS who may benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy; however, these patients are part of broader studies on the treatment of STS and those with LMS are not the primary study population.6,9There are few data on advanced LMS, although most first-line regimens tend to include doxorubicin-based therapy.6 This patient’s case was discussed among the tumor board and given positive margins and a high-grade pathology; she received adjuvant proton radiotherapy to the margin edge with close monitoring for recurrence. This case reflects the importance of close monitoring of patients with a history of hereditary retinoblastoma, with a particular emphasis on screening for bone and STS as well as melanoma. Current expert recommendation includes an annual physical examination at a long-term survivor clinic, patient education, and consideration of screening whole-body magnetic resonance imaging.10

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: The patient underwent a transvenous biopsy with an inferior vena cava filter, and pathology results were consistent with a leiomyosarcoma (LMS), grade 3. Computed tomography results of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were negative for metastatic disease. She subsequently underwent a radical resection of the pelvic mass, which revealed a 4-cm mass deriving from and encapsulating the right external iliac vein with R1 margins, which was replaced with an interposition graft. Retinoblastoma is the most common pediatric ocular tumor. The hereditary variant, which is caused by germline variations to the tumor suppressor geneRB1,comprises 40% of all retinoblastoma and is generally associated with bilateral disease.1Long-term survival of these patients is typically excellent; however, there remains a 33.1% risk of developing a secondary cancer.2,3This has important implications for monitoring survivors of hereditary retinoblastoma. The median time to development of a subsequent cancer is 18.9 years, and bone and soft-tissue sarcomas comprise most (40%-60%) subsequent cancers, followed by melanoma, accounting for approximately 10%.3Among soft-tissue sarcomas (STS), LMS is most common, comprising at least 40% of all STS diagnosed in patients with retinoblastoma with a median age at presentation of approximately 32 years.3Other commonly diagnosed subsequent STS include fibrosarcoma, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.3Prior treatment with radiation or chemotherapy may increase the risk of a subsequent cancer.4Radiotherapy is a risk factor for developing a subsequent cancer within the treatment field, and alkylating agents, in particular, seem to increase systemic risk of subsequent cancer. Patients who were treated with radiotherapy and an alkylating agent before age 1 year, as with this patient, may have up to 3.8 times greater risk of developing LMS.4 Leiomyosarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumor that is typically found in the head, neck, thorax, abdomen, retroperitoneum, limbs, uterus, and pelvis of patients with retinoblastoma.3Leiomyosarcoma of large blood vessels comprises approximately 2% of LMS and is often found in the inferior vena cava, femoral, saphenous, jugular, or iliac veins.5 Prognosis is based on histologic grade, tumor size, and tumor depth.6Extrauterine LMS has a 40% 5-year risk of recurrence following resection, and for uterine LMS, the recurrence rates are as high as 70%.6To our knowledge, there are few studies to guide optimal treatment of early-stage disease. Surgical resection is the standard for local disease, and offers a chance at a cure with R0 resection.6Adjuvant radiotherapy in early-stage disease has been shown to decrease the risk of local recurrence; however, a recent large, randomized clinical trial of patients with retroperitoneal LMS demonstrated a limited utility of adjuvant radiotherapy.6,7Adjuvant chemotherapy has not been shown to improve outcomes for patients with uterine LMS.8There have been studies that attempt to risk stratify and identify patients with nonuterine LMS who may benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy; however, these patients are part of broader studies on the treatment of STS and those with LMS are not the primary study population.6,9There are few data on advanced LMS, although most first-line regimens tend to include doxorubicin-based therapy.6 This patient’s case was discussed among the tumor board and given positive margins and a high-grade pathology; she received adjuvant proton radiotherapy to the margin edge with close monitoring for recurrence. This case reflects the importance of close monitoring of patients with a history of hereditary retinoblastoma, with a particular emphasis on screening for bone and STS as well as melanoma. Current expert recommendation includes an annual physical examination at a long-term survivor clinic, patient education, and consideration of screening whole-body magnetic resonance imaging.10

   Definition:

case_info.caption: Computed tomography venogram demonstrating a 4.0 × 3.5 cm heterogeneously enhancing lobulated mass (arrowhead) extending into the right common iliac vein.
case_info.explanation: The patient underwent a transvenous biopsy with an inferior vena cava filter, and pathology results were consistent with a leiomyosarcoma (LMS), grade 3. Computed tomography results of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were negative for metastatic disease. She subsequently underwent a radical resection of the pelvic mass, which revealed a 4-cm mass deriving from and encapsulating the right external iliac vein with R1 margins, which was replaced with an interposition graft. Retinoblastoma is the most common pediatric ocular tumor. The hereditary variant, which is caused by germline variations to the tumor suppressor geneRB1,comprises 40% of all retinoblastoma and is generally associated with bilateral disease.1Long-term survival of these patients is typically excellent; however, there remains a 33.1% risk of developing a secondary cancer.2,3This has important implications for monitoring survivors of hereditary retinoblastoma. The median time to development of a subsequent cancer is 18.9 years, and bone and soft-tissue sarcomas comprise most (40%-60%) subsequent cancers, followed by melanoma, accounting for approximately 10%.3Among soft-tissue sarcomas (STS), LMS is most common, comprising at least 40% of all STS diagnosed in patients with retinoblastoma with a median age at presentation of approximately 32 years.3Other commonly diagnosed subsequent STS include fibrosarcoma, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.3Prior treatment with radiation or chemotherapy may increase the risk of a subsequent cancer.4Radiotherapy is a risk factor for developing a subsequent cancer within the treatment field, and alkylating agents, in particular, seem to increase systemic risk of subsequent cancer. Patients who were treated with radiotherapy and an alkylating agent before age 1 year, as with this patient, may have up to 3.8 times greater risk of developing LMS.4 Leiomyosarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumor that is typically found in the head, neck, thorax, abdomen, retroperitoneum, limbs, uterus, and pelvis of patients with retinoblastoma.3Leiomyosarcoma of large blood vessels comprises approximately 2% of LMS and is often found in the inferior vena cava, femoral, saphenous, jugular, or iliac veins.5 Prognosis is based on histologic grade, tumor size, and tumor depth.6Extrauterine LMS has a 40% 5-year risk of recurrence following resection, and for uterine LMS, the recurrence rates are as high as 70%.6To our knowledge, there are few studies to guide optimal treatment of early-stage disease. Surgical resection is the standard for local disease, and offers a chance at a cure with R0 resection.6Adjuvant radiotherapy in early-stage disease has been shown to decrease the risk of local recurrence; however, a recent large, randomized clinical trial of patients with retroperitoneal LMS demonstrated a limited utility of adjuvant radiotherapy.6,7Adjuvant chemotherapy has not been shown to improve outcomes for patients with uterine LMS.8There have been studies that attempt to risk stratify and identify patients with nonuterine LMS who may benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy; however, these patients are part of broader studies on the treatment of STS and those with LMS are not the primary study population.6,9There are few data on advanced LMS, although most first-line regimens tend to include doxorubicin-based therapy.6 This patient’s case was discussed among the tumor board and given positive margins and a high-grade pathology; she received adjuvant proton radiotherapy to the margin edge with close monitoring for recurrence. This case reflects the importance of close monitoring of patients with a history of hereditary retinoblastoma, with a particular emphasis on screening for bone and STS as well as melanoma. Current expert recommendation includes an annual physical examination at a long-term survivor clinic, patient education, and consideration of screening whole-body magnetic resonance imaging.10

At age 8 months, she was treated with right enucleation and left eye radiotherapy (50.4 Gy). At age 4 years, she developed a recurrence of the retinoblastoma in the nasal cavity and was treated with 4 cycles of vincristine, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide followed by 1 cycle of cisplatin, etoposide, and intrathecal cytarabine. Primary care evaluation was prompted by her mother, as the patient had not noticed her lower extremity edema. She had no fevers, weight loss, shortness of breath, chest pain, abdominal pain, or history of deep vein thrombosis. Her physical examination was notable for firm, nonpitting edema to the hip. She did not have any associated tenderness, inguinal lymphadenopathy, or palpable abdominal masses. Her vital signs were within normal limits and she ambulated comfortably. Laboratory work results, including a complete blood cell count with a differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, and D-dimer levels, were within normal limits. case_info.caption: Computed tomography venogram demonstrating a 4.0 × 3.5 cm heterogeneously enhancing lobulated mass (arrowhead) extending into the right common iliac vein.
case_info.explanation: The patient underwent a transvenous biopsy with an inferior vena cava filter, and pathology results were consistent with a leiomyosarcoma (LMS), grade 3. Computed tomography results of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were negative for metastatic disease. She subsequently underwent a radical resection of the pelvic mass, which revealed a 4-cm mass deriving from and encapsulating the right external iliac vein with R1 margins, which was replaced with an interposition graft. Retinoblastoma is the most common pediatric ocular tumor. The hereditary variant, which is caused by germline variations to the tumor suppressor geneRB1,comprises 40% of all retinoblastoma and is generally associated with bilateral disease.1Long-term survival of these patients is typically excellent; however, there remains a 33.1% risk of developing a secondary cancer.2,3This has important implications for monitoring survivors of hereditary retinoblastoma. The median time to development of a subsequent cancer is 18.9 years, and bone and soft-tissue sarcomas comprise most (40%-60%) subsequent cancers, followed by melanoma, accounting for approximately 10%.3Among soft-tissue sarcomas (STS), LMS is most common, comprising at least 40% of all STS diagnosed in patients with retinoblastoma with a median age at presentation of approximately 32 years.3Other commonly diagnosed subsequent STS include fibrosarcoma, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.3Prior treatment with radiation or chemotherapy may increase the risk of a subsequent cancer.4Radiotherapy is a risk factor for developing a subsequent cancer within the treatment field, and alkylating agents, in particular, seem to increase systemic risk of subsequent cancer. Patients who were treated with radiotherapy and an alkylating agent before age 1 year, as with this patient, may have up to 3.8 times greater risk of developing LMS.4 Leiomyosarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumor that is typically found in the head, neck, thorax, abdomen, retroperitoneum, limbs, uterus, and pelvis of patients with retinoblastoma.3Leiomyosarcoma of large blood vessels comprises approximately 2% of LMS and is often found in the inferior vena cava, femoral, saphenous, jugular, or iliac veins.5 Prognosis is based on histologic grade, tumor size, and tumor depth.6Extrauterine LMS has a 40% 5-year risk of recurrence following resection, and for uterine LMS, the recurrence rates are as high as 70%.6To our knowledge, there are few studies to guide optimal treatment of early-stage disease. Surgical resection is the standard for local disease, and offers a chance at a cure with R0 resection.6Adjuvant radiotherapy in early-stage disease has been shown to decrease the risk of local recurrence; however, a recent large, randomized clinical trial of patients with retroperitoneal LMS demonstrated a limited utility of adjuvant radiotherapy.6,7Adjuvant chemotherapy has not been shown to improve outcomes for patients with uterine LMS.8There have been studies that attempt to risk stratify and identify patients with nonuterine LMS who may benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy; however, these patients are part of broader studies on the treatment of STS and those with LMS are not the primary study population.6,9There are few data on advanced LMS, although most first-line regimens tend to include doxorubicin-based therapy.6 This patient’s case was discussed among the tumor board and given positive margins and a high-grade pathology; she received adjuvant proton radiotherapy to the margin edge with close monitoring for recurrence. This case reflects the importance of close monitoring of patients with a history of hereditary retinoblastoma, with a particular emphasis on screening for bone and STS as well as melanoma. Current expert recommendation includes an annual physical examination at a long-term survivor clinic, patient education, and consideration of screening whole-body magnetic resonance imaging.10

She subsequently underwent a radical resection of the pelvic mass, which revealed a 4-cm mass deriving from and encapsulating the right external iliac vein with R1 margins, which was replaced with an interposition graft. Retinoblastoma is the most common pediatric ocular tumor. The hereditary variant, which is caused by germline variations to the tumor suppressor geneRB1,comprises 40% of all retinoblastoma and is generally associated with bilateral disease.1Long-term survival of these patients is typically excellent; however, there remains a 33.1% risk of developing a secondary cancer.2,3This has important implications for monitoring survivors of hereditary retinoblastoma. The median time to development of a subsequent cancer is 18.9 years, and bone and soft-tissue sarcomas comprise most (40%-60%) subsequent cancers, followed by melanoma, accounting for approximately 10%.3Among soft-tissue sarcomas (STS), LMS is most common, comprising at least 40% of all STS diagnosed in patients with retinoblastoma with a median age at presentation of approximately 32 years.3Other commonly diagnosed subsequent STS include fibrosarcoma, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.3Prior treatment with radiation or chemotherapy may increase the risk of a subsequent cancer.4Radiotherapy is a risk factor for developing a subsequent cancer within the treatment field, and alkylating agents, in particular, seem to increase systemic risk of subsequent cancer. Patients who were treated with radiotherapy and an alkylating agent before age 1 year, as with this patient, may have up to 3.8 times greater risk of developing LMS.4 Leiomyosarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumor that is typically found in the head, neck, thorax, abdomen, retroperitoneum, limbs, uterus, and pelvis of patients with retinoblastoma.3Leiomyosarcoma of large blood vessels comprises approximately 2% of LMS and is often found in the inferior vena cava, femoral, saphenous, jugular, or iliac veins.5 Prognosis is based on histologic grade, tumor size, and tumor depth.6Extrauterine LMS has a 40% 5-year risk of recurrence following resection, and for uterine LMS, the recurrence rates are as high as 70%.6To our knowledge, there are few studies to guide optimal treatment of early-stage disease. Surgical resection is the standard for local disease, and offers a chance at a cure with R0 resection.6Adjuvant radiotherapy in early-stage disease has been shown to decrease the risk of local recurrence; however, a recent large, randomized clinical trial of patients with retroperitoneal LMS demonstrated a limited utility of adjuvant radiotherapy.6,7Adjuvant chemotherapy has not been shown to improve outcomes for patients with uterine LMS.8There have been studies that attempt to risk stratify and identify patients with nonuterine LMS who may benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy; however, these patients are part of broader studies on the treatment of STS and those with LMS are not the primary study population.6,9There are few data on advanced LMS, although most first-line regimens tend to include doxorubicin-based therapy.6 This patient’s case was discussed among the tumor board and given positive margins and a high-grade pathology; she received adjuvant proton radiotherapy to the margin edge with close monitoring for recurrence. This case reflects the importance of close monitoring of patients with a history of hereditary retinoblastoma, with a particular emphasis on screening for bone and STS as well as melanoma. Current expert recommendation includes an annual physical examination at a long-term survivor clinic, patient education, and consideration of screening whole-body magnetic resonance imaging.10

Laboratory work results, including a complete blood cell count with a differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, and D-dimer levels, were within normal limits. Doppler ultrasonography of her right lower extremity showed no deep vein thrombosis. Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:

* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

At age 8 months, she was treated with right enucleation and left eye radiotherapy (50.4 Gy). At age 4 years, she developed a recurrence of the retinoblastoma in the nasal cavity and was treated with 4 cycles of vincristine, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide followed by 1 cycle of cisplatin, etoposide, and intrathecal cytarabine. Primary care evaluation was prompted by her mother, as the patient had not noticed her lower extremity edema. She had no fevers, weight loss, shortness of breath, chest pain, abdominal pain, or history of deep vein thrombosis. Her physical examination was notable for firm, nonpitting edema to the hip. She did not have any associated tenderness, inguinal lymphadenopathy, or palpable abdominal masses. Her vital signs were within normal limits and she ambulated comfortably. Laboratory work results, including a complete blood cell count with a differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, and D-dimer levels, were within normal limits. case_info.caption: Computed tomography venogram demonstrating a 4.0 × 3.5 cm heterogeneously enhancing lobulated mass (arrowhead) extending into the right common iliac vein.
case_info.explanation: The patient underwent a transvenous biopsy with an inferior vena cava filter, and pathology results were consistent with a leiomyosarcoma (LMS), grade 3. Computed tomography results of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were negative for metastatic disease. She subsequently underwent a radical resection of the pelvic mass, which revealed a 4-cm mass deriving from and encapsulating the right external iliac vein with R1 margins, which was replaced with an interposition graft. Retinoblastoma is the most common pediatric ocular tumor. The hereditary variant, which is caused by germline variations to the tumor suppressor geneRB1,comprises 40% of all retinoblastoma and is generally associated with bilateral disease.1Long-term survival of these patients is typically excellent; however, there remains a 33.1% risk of developing a secondary cancer.2,3This has important implications for monitoring survivors of hereditary retinoblastoma. The median time to development of a subsequent cancer is 18.9 years, and bone and soft-tissue sarcomas comprise most (40%-60%) subsequent cancers, followed by melanoma, accounting for approximately 10%.3Among soft-tissue sarcomas (STS), LMS is most common, comprising at least 40% of all STS diagnosed in patients with retinoblastoma with a median age at presentation of approximately 32 years.3Other commonly diagnosed subsequent STS include fibrosarcoma, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.3Prior treatment with radiation or chemotherapy may increase the risk of a subsequent cancer.4Radiotherapy is a risk factor for developing a subsequent cancer within the treatment field, and alkylating agents, in particular, seem to increase systemic risk of subsequent cancer. Patients who were treated with radiotherapy and an alkylating agent before age 1 year, as with this patient, may have up to 3.8 times greater risk of developing LMS.4 Leiomyosarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumor that is typically found in the head, neck, thorax, abdomen, retroperitoneum, limbs, uterus, and pelvis of patients with retinoblastoma.3Leiomyosarcoma of large blood vessels comprises approximately 2% of LMS and is often found in the inferior vena cava, femoral, saphenous, jugular, or iliac veins.5 Prognosis is based on histologic grade, tumor size, and tumor depth.6Extrauterine LMS has a 40% 5-year risk of recurrence following resection, and for uterine LMS, the recurrence rates are as high as 70%.6To our knowledge, there are few studies to guide optimal treatment of early-stage disease. Surgical resection is the standard for local disease, and offers a chance at a cure with R0 resection.6Adjuvant radiotherapy in early-stage disease has been shown to decrease the risk of local recurrence; however, a recent large, randomized clinical trial of patients with retroperitoneal LMS demonstrated a limited utility of adjuvant radiotherapy.6,7Adjuvant chemotherapy has not been shown to improve outcomes for patients with uterine LMS.8There have been studies that attempt to risk stratify and identify patients with nonuterine LMS who may benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy; however, these patients are part of broader studies on the treatment of STS and those with LMS are not the primary study population.6,9There are few data on advanced LMS, although most first-line regimens tend to include doxorubicin-based therapy.6 This patient’s case was discussed among the tumor board and given positive margins and a high-grade pathology; she received adjuvant proton radiotherapy to the margin edge with close monitoring for recurrence. This case reflects the importance of close monitoring of patients with a history of hereditary retinoblastoma, with a particular emphasis on screening for bone and STS as well as melanoma. Current expert recommendation includes an annual physical examination at a long-term survivor clinic, patient education, and consideration of screening whole-body magnetic resonance imaging.10

At age 8 months, she was treated with right enucleation and left eye radiotherapy (50.4 Gy). At age 4 years, she developed a recurrence of the retinoblastoma in the nasal cavity and was treated with 4 cycles of vincristine, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide followed by 1 cycle of cisplatin, etoposide, and intrathecal cytarabine. Primary care evaluation was prompted by her mother, as the patient had not noticed her lower extremity edema. She had no fevers, weight loss, shortness of breath, chest pain, abdominal pain, or history of deep vein thrombosis. Her physical examination was notable for firm, nonpitting edema to the hip. She did not have any associated tenderness, inguinal lymphadenopathy, or palpable abdominal masses. Her vital signs were within normal limits and she ambulated comfortably. Laboratory work results, including a complete blood cell count with a differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, and D-dimer levels, were within normal limits. case_info.caption: Computed tomography venogram demonstrating a 4.0 × 3.5 cm heterogeneously enhancing lobulated mass (arrowhead) extending into the right common iliac vein.
case_info.explanation: The patient underwent a transvenous biopsy with an inferior vena cava filter, and pathology results were consistent with a leiomyosarcoma (LMS), grade 3. Computed tomography results of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were negative for metastatic disease. She subsequently underwent a radical resection of the pelvic mass, which revealed a 4-cm mass deriving from and encapsulating the right external iliac vein with R1 margins, which was replaced with an interposition graft. Retinoblastoma is the most common pediatric ocular tumor. The hereditary variant, which is caused by germline variations to the tumor suppressor geneRB1,comprises 40% of all retinoblastoma and is generally associated with bilateral disease.1Long-term survival of these patients is typically excellent; however, there remains a 33.1% risk of developing a secondary cancer.2,3This has important implications for monitoring survivors of hereditary retinoblastoma. The median time to development of a subsequent cancer is 18.9 years, and bone and soft-tissue sarcomas comprise most (40%-60%) subsequent cancers, followed by melanoma, accounting for approximately 10%.3Among soft-tissue sarcomas (STS), LMS is most common, comprising at least 40% of all STS diagnosed in patients with retinoblastoma with a median age at presentation of approximately 32 years.3Other commonly diagnosed subsequent STS include fibrosarcoma, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.3Prior treatment with radiation or chemotherapy may increase the risk of a subsequent cancer.4Radiotherapy is a risk factor for developing a subsequent cancer within the treatment field, and alkylating agents, in particular, seem to increase systemic risk of subsequent cancer. Patients who were treated with radiotherapy and an alkylating agent before age 1 year, as with this patient, may have up to 3.8 times greater risk of developing LMS.4 Leiomyosarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumor that is typically found in the head, neck, thorax, abdomen, retroperitoneum, limbs, uterus, and pelvis of patients with retinoblastoma.3Leiomyosarcoma of large blood vessels comprises approximately 2% of LMS and is often found in the inferior vena cava, femoral, saphenous, jugular, or iliac veins.5 Prognosis is based on histologic grade, tumor size, and tumor depth.6Extrauterine LMS has a 40% 5-year risk of recurrence following resection, and for uterine LMS, the recurrence rates are as high as 70%.6To our knowledge, there are few studies to guide optimal treatment of early-stage disease. Surgical resection is the standard for local disease, and offers a chance at a cure with R0 resection.6Adjuvant radiotherapy in early-stage disease has been shown to decrease the risk of local recurrence; however, a recent large, randomized clinical trial of patients with retroperitoneal LMS demonstrated a limited utility of adjuvant radiotherapy.6,7Adjuvant chemotherapy has not been shown to improve outcomes for patients with uterine LMS.8There have been studies that attempt to risk stratify and identify patients with nonuterine LMS who may benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy; however, these patients are part of broader studies on the treatment of STS and those with LMS are not the primary study population.6,9There are few data on advanced LMS, although most first-line regimens tend to include doxorubicin-based therapy.6 This patient’s case was discussed among the tumor board and given positive margins and a high-grade pathology; she received adjuvant proton radiotherapy to the margin edge with close monitoring for recurrence. This case reflects the importance of close monitoring of patients with a history of hereditary retinoblastoma, with a particular emphasis on screening for bone and STS as well as melanoma. Current expert recommendation includes an annual physical examination at a long-term survivor clinic, patient education, and consideration of screening whole-body magnetic resonance imaging.10

case_info.caption: Computed tomography venogram demonstrating a 4.0 × 3.5 cm heterogeneously enhancing lobulated mass (arrowhead) extending into the right common iliac vein.
case_info.explanation: The patient underwent a transvenous biopsy with an inferior vena cava filter, and pathology results were consistent with a leiomyosarcoma (LMS), grade 3. Computed tomography results of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were negative for metastatic disease. She subsequently underwent a radical resection of the pelvic mass, which revealed a 4-cm mass deriving from and encapsulating the right external iliac vein with R1 margins, which was replaced with an interposition graft. Retinoblastoma is the most common pediatric ocular tumor. The hereditary variant, which is caused by germline variations to the tumor suppressor geneRB1,comprises 40% of all retinoblastoma and is generally associated with bilateral disease.1Long-term survival of these patients is typically excellent; however, there remains a 33.1% risk of developing a secondary cancer.2,3This has important implications for monitoring survivors of hereditary retinoblastoma. The median time to development of a subsequent cancer is 18.9 years, and bone and soft-tissue sarcomas comprise most (40%-60%) subsequent cancers, followed by melanoma, accounting for approximately 10%.3Among soft-tissue sarcomas (STS), LMS is most common, comprising at least 40% of all STS diagnosed in patients with retinoblastoma with a median age at presentation of approximately 32 years.3Other commonly diagnosed subsequent STS include fibrosarcoma, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.3Prior treatment with radiation or chemotherapy may increase the risk of a subsequent cancer.4Radiotherapy is a risk factor for developing a subsequent cancer within the treatment field, and alkylating agents, in particular, seem to increase systemic risk of subsequent cancer. Patients who were treated with radiotherapy and an alkylating agent before age 1 year, as with this patient, may have up to 3.8 times greater risk of developing LMS.4 Leiomyosarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumor that is typically found in the head, neck, thorax, abdomen, retroperitoneum, limbs, uterus, and pelvis of patients with retinoblastoma.3Leiomyosarcoma of large blood vessels comprises approximately 2% of LMS and is often found in the inferior vena cava, femoral, saphenous, jugular, or iliac veins.5 Prognosis is based on histologic grade, tumor size, and tumor depth.6Extrauterine LMS has a 40% 5-year risk of recurrence following resection, and for uterine LMS, the recurrence rates are as high as 70%.6To our knowledge, there are few studies to guide optimal treatment of early-stage disease. Surgical resection is the standard for local disease, and offers a chance at a cure with R0 resection.6Adjuvant radiotherapy in early-stage disease has been shown to decrease the risk of local recurrence; however, a recent large, randomized clinical trial of patients with retroperitoneal LMS demonstrated a limited utility of adjuvant radiotherapy.6,7Adjuvant chemotherapy has not been shown to improve outcomes for patients with uterine LMS.8There have been studies that attempt to risk stratify and identify patients with nonuterine LMS who may benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy; however, these patients are part of broader studies on the treatment of STS and those with LMS are not the primary study population.6,9There are few data on advanced LMS, although most first-line regimens tend to include doxorubicin-based therapy.6 This patient’s case was discussed among the tumor board and given positive margins and a high-grade pathology; she received adjuvant proton radiotherapy to the margin edge with close monitoring for recurrence. This case reflects the importance of close monitoring of patients with a history of hereditary retinoblastoma, with a particular emphasis on screening for bone and STS as well as melanoma. Current expert recommendation includes an annual physical examination at a long-term survivor clinic, patient education, and consideration of screening whole-body magnetic resonance imaging.10
